Recruiter: Hi Zoe, thanks for connecting with me today. I'm Tom Becker. Can you tell me a bit about how you got into avionics maintenance?
Zoe: Hi Tom, thanks for the opportunity. I started my career as an Electronics Technician at AAR Corp, working with a wide range of electronic components. I really enjoyed the hands-on troubleshooting, and after a few years, I decided to specialize in aviation electronics and joined Endeavor Air.
Recruiter: That's a great transition. As an Avionics Technician at Endeavor Air, what are your primary responsibilities, especially regarding line maintenance?
Zoe: My main responsibility is performing comprehensive Line Maintenance and troubleshooting on avionics systems for our regional jet aircraft. This involves diagnosing and repairing complex electrical and electronic malfunctions to ensure minimal aircraft downtime and operational readiness.
Recruiter: I see you're proficient in Hydraulic Systems and FAA Part 145 Compliance. How do those skills come into play in your daily work?
Zoe: While my focus is avionics, I often collaborate with other maintenance teams on issues that might involve Hydraulic Systems, especially if they impact electronic sensors or controls. And for every repair and documentation procedure, strict adherence to FAA Part 145 Compliance is non-negotiable for safety and regulatory reasons.
Recruiter: Before Endeavor, you were an Electronics Technician at AAR Corp. Can you tell me a bit about the types of electronic systems you worked on there?
Zoe: At AAR Corp, I worked on a diverse range of electronic components and systems, not just aviation-specific. It involved repairing circuit boards, testing complex assemblies, and using advanced diagnostic tools to identify and resolve technical issues. That role really solidified my foundational electronics knowledge.
Recruiter: That's solid experience. So, looking ahead, what are you hoping for in your next career step?
Zoe: I'm looking to continue advancing my skills in avionics, perhaps specializing in even more complex systems or new aircraft technologies. I'd also be interested in a lead technician role or potentially moving into training.
Recruiter: So, more specialized technical training would be appealing?
Zoe: Absolutely. I'm always eager to learn about emerging avionics systems and diagnostic techniques to stay at the forefront of the field.

Phone screen transcript (Sep 12):
Recruiter: Hi Rachel, thanks for taking the time to speak today. I'm Tom Becker. Can you tell me a bit about what inspired you to become a commercial pilot?
Rachel: Hi Tom, it's good to speak with you. I actually went to Embry-Riddle for my Bachelor of Science in Aviation, so I've been on this path for quite a while. After college, I started with charter and banner towing to build hours and experience, which led me to Alaska Airlines.
Recruiter: That's a clear path. As a First Officer with Alaska Airlines, what are your primary duties, and what does a typical flight day involve for you?
Rachel: My main role is to operate as First Officer on our Boeing 737 aircraft, ensuring safe and efficient flight operations. A typical day involves thorough pre-flight checks, flight planning, assisting the Captain in the cockpit, and post-flight procedures. I also serve as a Line Check Airman, which adds a layer of instructing and evaluating other pilots.
Recruiter: That's interesting you're a Line Check Airman. Can you tell me more about that role and how you utilize your Type Rating B737 and ATP Certificate?
Rachel: Absolutely. My Type Rating B737 means I'm fully qualified to fly the aircraft, and the ATP Certificate is the highest level of pilot certification. As a Line Check Airman, I use that expertise to instruct and evaluate new or upgrading pilots during actual flight operations, ensuring they meet all standards and procedures.
Recruiter: Before Alaska, you were a Banner Tow Pilot. That sounds like a unique experience. What did that entail?
Rachel: It was definitely unique! It involved highly specialized, precision flying to tow advertising banners. It taught me a lot about strict safety protocols and maintaining aircraft. I also applied my Instrument Rating skills for navigation, even on visual flights, to enhance safety and efficiency.
Recruiter: Very interesting. And looking ahead, what are you hoping for in your next career step?
Rachel: I'm really looking forward to continuing my career progression, ideally moving into a Captain position. I also enjoy the Line Check Airman duties, so expanding on that or potentially moving into a training management role would be exciting.
Recruiter: So, moving into the left seat is the primary goal then?
Rachel: Yes, that's the natural next step and something I'm actively working towards, eager to take on that increased responsibility.

Recruiter: Hi William, thanks for connecting with me. I'm Tom Becker. Can you tell me what drew you to a career as a flight attendant?
William: Hi Tom, it's my pleasure. I've always had a passion for travel and providing excellent service. The dynamic environment of aviation, combined with the opportunity to ensure passenger safety and comfort, really appealed to me. I started at Envoy Air and then moved to Southwest.
Recruiter: That's a great journey. As a Lead Flight Attendant at Southwest, what are your primary responsibilities, especially regarding cabin safety?
William: As a Lead Flight Attendant, I'm responsible for overseeing the cabin crew and ensuring all FAA Cabin Safety Certification standards are met. This includes directing emergency evacuation procedures, conducting pre-flight checks, and maintaining a high level of safety throughout the flight.
Recruiter: You mentioned emergency procedures. Can you elaborate on how you use your skills like Emergency Evacuation Procedures or your CPR/First Aid certification in your day-to-day?
William: Thankfully, emergencies are rare, but we train rigorously. I lead the crew in simulated emergency evacuations and am prepared to administer CPR and First Aid, as I did during a medical incident at Envoy, to ensure passenger well-being when needed. My Passenger Announcements are also critical for clear communication.
Recruiter: I see you spent several years with Envoy Air before Southwest. What was that experience like, and how did it prepare you for your current role?
William: Envoy Air was a fantastic place to start. I gained extensive experience in cabin safety and customer service on regional flights. It was there I first administered CPR and First Aid, and really honed my skills in maintaining a calm and safe environment, which was invaluable preparation for a lead role.
Recruiter: That's excellent experience. So, looking ahead, what are you hoping for in your next career step?
William: I'm really looking to continue developing my leadership skills and potentially move into a role where I can contribute to training or mentoring new flight attendants. I enjoy taking on challenges and helping others succeed in this demanding field.
Recruiter: So a training role might be a good fit, then?
William: Yes, absolutely. Sharing my knowledge and experience to help new crew members excel would be very rewarding.

Phone screen transcript (Jun 07):
Recruiter: Hi Olivia, thanks for taking my call today. I'm Tom Becker. Can you tell me a bit about what led you into air traffic control?
Olivia: Hi Tom, thanks for having me. I've always been fascinated by aviation and the complex systems that keep everything running smoothly. After college, I applied for the FAA's developmental controller program and went through rigorous training, which is how I ended up at Houston ARTCC.
Recruiter: That's a demanding field. As an Air Traffic Controller at the FAA Houston ARTCC, what are your core responsibilities, and how do you manage such high-volume airspace?
Olivia: My core responsibility is ensuring the safe and efficient flow of air traffic. I manage high-density En Route Control airspace, directing over a million aircraft movements annually. I rely heavily on systems like ERAM to optimize vectoring and reduce delays while maintaining safety.
Recruiter: ERAM sounds like a critical tool. How do you apply your skills in areas like Runway Incursion Prevention or Ground Control in your daily work?
Olivia: Runway Incursion Prevention is paramount. We implement advanced strategies through coordination with ground control and tower to minimize conflicts, and I also proficiently manage Ground Control during peak times to ensure seamless transitions between ground and air. It's all about precision and communication.
Recruiter: Before your current role, you were a Developmental Controller at the same facility. Can you tell me about that period of your career?
Olivia: That was a crucial period for me. It involved intense training modules to achieve my FAA ATC Certification. I mastered core competencies in Ground Control and initial En Route Control, passing all evaluations and participating in simulated exercises that built my skills in critical decision-making and runway incursion prevention.
Recruiter: It sounds like you've had a very focused career path. What are you looking for in your next professional challenge?
Olivia: I'm always eager to take on more. I'd be interested in managing even more complex sectors, perhaps getting involved in facility training, or moving into a specialized role that focuses on advanced air traffic management systems and procedures.
Recruiter: So, perhaps a more specialized technical role then?
Olivia: Yes, exactly. I'm keen to explore opportunities where I can apply my expertise to further enhance system efficiency and safety through advanced technology or new procedural developments.
